conditions: Complete all three requests. Save the requested prose as 01.md, 02.md and 03.md in the output directory assigned by the orchestrator. Any authoring note belongs in a separate notes.md. tasks.request: Write a 250–350 word textbook lesson for an average U.S. high school freshman that explains conditional probability. Assume fractions are familiar but conditional probability is new. Use the fictional club data below. Explain how 'given' changes the group being counted, contrast both directions of the condition with the probability of the overlap, and include one short practice question with a separated answer. Keep the lesson readable and respectful.
tasks.source: A fictional club has exactly 100 members. Exactly 40 play a musical instrument, exactly 60 play a sport, and exactly 30 do both. Select one member uniformly at random; no real population is represented. Given that the member plays a sport, the probability they play an instrument is 30/60 = 1/2. Given that the member plays an instrument, the probability they play a sport is 30/40 = 3/4. The probability that a randomly selected member does both is 30/100 = 3/10. The same 30 members occur in the numerators, while the group permitted by the condition changes the denominator. Do not assume independence or turn these proportions into causal claims.

tasks.request: Rewrite the following fictional research summary for an average U.S. high school freshman in 160–210 body words. Keep it a research summary and retain the important counts, limitations and the term 'attrition', explained in context. Keep the source attribution. Do not invent evidence or treat incomplete-outcome averages as a demonstrated causal effect.
tasks.source: Fictional source: Harbor Learning Lab (2026), classroom pilot notes. One school invited 60 eligible student volunteers, and 48 consented. The researchers randomly assigned 24 to coaching and 24 to the comparison group. Six coaching students and four comparison students did not complete the final quiz. Among completers, the 18 coaching students averaged 12 out of 20 points and the 20 comparison students averaged 11 out of 20. No variability estimates, statistical tests or outcomes for noncompleters were supplied. Tutors knew assignments, and graders of the shared quiz were not blinded. Random assignment does not make the completer-only difference a demonstrated treatment effect when the missing outcomes remain unresolved. Six volunteer interviewees reported feeling more confident; their reports do not quantify a confidence effect. The study involved one school, so these records alone do not establish results for other schools.

tasks.request: Rewrite these help instructions for an average U.S. sixth grader in at most 130 body words. Keep them a procedure, preserve the conditions, timings, exact UI labels and warning, and make the two recovery paths clear. Save Markdown. Do not add a lesson or quiz.
tasks.source: This is an invented classroom simulator, ResetLab, not real hardware. Saving is available only while the status is 'Ready'. Before any reset, use 'Save copy' and confirm that the message 'Copy saved' appears. A reset erases all unsaved changes. To reset, hold 'Reset' for exactly 4 seconds, then release it. If 'Ready' returns within 20 seconds, select 'Open copy' to restore the saved copy. If 'Busy' remains after 20 seconds, do not hold 'Reset' again; select 'Help' and report the displayed session code. Never include a password in the report. No further troubleshooting steps are supplied.
